{{Short description|Radius of a circle or sphere equivalent to a non-circular or non-spherical object}}
{{redirect|Mean radius|the usage in astronomy|mean radius (astronomy)}}

In [[applied science]]s, the '''equivalent radius''' (or '''mean radius''') is the radius of a circle or sphere with the same perimeter, area, or volume of a non-circular or non-spherical object. The '''equivalent diameter''' (or '''mean diameter''') (<math>D</math>) is twice the equivalent radius.

==Perimeter equivalent==
[[Image:Using a DTApe.JPG|thumb|right|200px|Measurement of tree circumference. The tape is calibrated to show diameter at breast height, assuming a circular shape.]]

The [[perimeter of a circle]] of radius ''R'' is <math>2 \pi R</math>. Given the perimeter of a non-circular object ''P'', one can calculate its '''perimeter-equivalent radius''' by setting
:<math>P = 2\pi R_\text{eq}</math>
or, alternatively:
:<math>R_\text{eq} = \frac{P}{2\pi}</math>

For example, a square of side ''L'' has a perimeter of <math>4L</math>. Setting that perimeter to be equal to that of a circle imply that
:<math>R_\text{eq} = \frac{4L}{2 \pi} = \frac{2L}{\pi} \approx 0.6366 L</math>

Applications:
* [[US hat size]] is the circumference of the head, measured in inches, divided by [[pi (constant)|pi]], rounded to the nearest 1/8 inch. This corresponds to the 1D mean diameter.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bello |first1=Ignacio |last2=Britton |first2=Jack Rolf |date=1993 |title=Topics in Contemporary Mathematics |edition=5th |page=512 |location=Lexington, Mass |publisher=D.C. Heath |isbn=978-0-669-28957-2}}</ref>
*[[Diameter at breast height]] is the circumference of [[tree trunk]], measured at height of 4.5 feet, divided by pi. This corresponds to the 1D mean diameter. It can be measured directly by a [[girthing tape]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=West |first1=P. W. |date=2004 |title=Tree and Forest Measurement |chapter=Stem diameter |pages=13ff |location=New York |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-540-40390-6 }}</ref>

==Area equivalent==
[[Image:Area-equivalent radius and diameter.svg|thumb|The area-equivalent radius of a 2D object is the radius of a circle with the same area as the object]]
[[Image:Wetted Perimeter.svg|thumb|Cross sectional area of a trapezoidal open channel, red highlights the [[wetted perimeter]], where water is in contact with the channel. The [[hydraulic diameter]] is the equivalent circular configuration with the same circumference as the wetted perimeter.]]

The [[area of a circle]] of radius ''R'' is <math>\pi R^2</math>. Given the area of a non-circular object ''A'', one can calculate its '''area-equivalent radius''' by setting
:<math>A = \pi R^2_\text{eq}</math>
or, alternatively:
:<math>R_\text{eq} = \sqrt{\frac{A}{\pi}}</math>
Often the area considered is that of a [[Cross section (geometry)|cross section]].

For example, a square of side length ''L'' has an area of <math>L^2</math>. Setting that area to be equal that of a circle imply that
:<math>R_\text{eq} = \sqrt{\frac{L^2}{\pi}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{\pi}} L \approx 0.5642 L</math>

Similarly, an [[ellipse]] with [[semi-major axis]] <math>a</math> and [[semi-minor axis]] <math>b</math> has area of <math>\pi ab</math>, and therefore
:<math>R_\text{eq} = \sqrt{\frac{\pi ab}{\pi}} = \sqrt{a b}</math>.

Applications:
*The [[hydraulic diameter]] is similarly defined as 4 times the [[cross-sectional area]] of a pipe ''A'', divided by its [[wetted perimeter|"wetted" perimeter]] ''P''. For a circular pipe of radius ''R'', at full flow, this is
:<math>D_\text{H} = \frac{4 \pi R^2}{2 \pi R} = 2R</math>
:as one would expect. This is equivalent to the above definition of the 2D mean diameter. However, for historical reasons, the [[hydraulic radius]] is defined as the cross-sectional area of a pipe ''A'', divided by its wetted perimeter ''P'', which leads to <math>D_\text{H} = 4 R_\text{H}</math>, and the hydraulic radius is ''half'' of the 2D mean radius.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Wei | first1=Maoxing | last2=Cheng | first2=Nian-Sheng | last3=Lu | first3=Yesheng | date=October 2023 | title=Revisiting the concept of hydraulic radius | journal=Journal of Hydrology | volume=625 |issue=Part B |article-number=130134 | doi=10.1016/j.jhydrol.2023.130134 | bibcode=2023JHyd..62530134W }}</ref>
*In [[Construction aggregate|aggregate]] classification, the equivalent diameter is the "diameter of a circle with an equal aggregate sectional area", which is calculated by <math>D = 2 \sqrt{\frac{A}{\pi}}</math>. It is used in many digital image processing programs.<ref>{{cite book | doi=10.1016/B978-0-12-849908-5.00013-4 | chapter=Asphalt mix homogeneity | title=Structural Behavior of Asphalt Pavements | date=2016 | last1=Sun | first1=Lijun | pages=821–921 | isbn=978-0-12-849908-5 }}</ref>

==Volume equivalent==
{{further|Mean radius (astronomy)|Equivalent spherical diameter}}
[[File:Ellipsoide.svg|thumb|right|300px|A sphere (top), rotational ellipsoid (left) and triaxial ellipsoid (right)]]

The [[volume of a sphere]] of radius ''R'' is <math>\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3</math>. Given the volume of a non-spherical object ''V'', one can calculate its '''volume-equivalent radius''' by setting
:<math>V = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3_\text{eq}</math>
or, alternatively:
:<math>R_\text{eq} = \sqrt[3]{\frac{3V}{4\pi}}</math>

For example, a cube of side length ''L'' has a volume of <math>L^3</math>. Setting that volume to be equal that of a sphere imply that
:<math>R_\text{eq} = \sqrt[3]{\frac{3L^3}{4\pi}} = \sqrt[3]{\frac{3}{4\pi}} L \approx 0.6204 L</math>

Similarly, a [[tri-axial ellipsoid]] with axes <math>a</math>, <math>b</math> and <math>c</math> has a volume of <math>\frac{4}{3}\pi abc</math>, and therefore<ref name="Leconte">{{cite journal|url=https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/pdf/2011/04/aa15811-10.pdf|title=Distorted, nonspherical transiting planets: impact on the transit depth and on the radius determination|first1=J.|last1=Leconte|first2=D.|last2=Lai|first3=G.|last3=Chabrier|journal=[[Astronomy & Astrophysics]]|volume=528|article-number=A41|year=2011|doi=10.1051/0004-6361/201015811|arxiv=1101.2813 |bibcode=2011A&A...528A..41L }}</ref>
:<math>R_\text{eq} = \sqrt[3]{\frac{3\frac{4}{3}\pi abc}{4\pi}} =\sqrt[3]{abc}</math>.
The formula for a [[rotational ellipsoid]] is the special case where <math>a=b</math>
:<math>R_\text{eq}=\sqrt[3]{a^{2} \cdot c }</math>.<ref name="Chambat"/>

Applications:
* For planet [[Earth]], which can be approximated as an oblate spheroid with radii {{val|6378.1|u=km}} and {{val|6356.8|u=km}}, the 3D mean radius is <math>R=\sqrt[3]{6378.1^{2}\cdot6356.8}=6371.0\text{ km}</math>.<ref name="Chambat">{{cite journal|url=http://frederic.chambat.free.fr/geophy/inertie_pepi01/chambat_valette_publie01_with_errata.pdf.pdf|title=Mean radius, mass, and inertia for reference Earth models|first1=F.|last1=Chambat|first2=B.|last2=Valette|journal=[[Physics of the Earth and Planetary Interiors]]|volume=124|issue=3–4|year=2001|page=4|doi=10.1016/S0031-9201(01)00200-X|bibcode=2001PEPI..124..237C }}</ref>

==Other equivalences==
===Surface-area equivalent radius===
{{See also|authalic radius}}

The [[surface area]] of a sphere of radius ''R'' is <math>4\pi R^2</math>. Given the surface area of a non-spherical object ''A'', one can calculate its surface area-equivalent radius by setting 
:<math>4\pi R^2_\text{eq} = A</math>

or equivalently
:<math>R_\text{eq} = \sqrt{\frac{A}{4\pi}}</math>

For example, a cube of length ''L'' has a surface area of <math>6L^2</math>.  A cube therefore has an surface area-equivalent radius of
:<math>R_\text{eq} = \sqrt{\frac{6L^2}{4\pi}} \approx 0.6910 L</math>

===Curvature-equivalent radius===
[[File:Osculating circle.svg|thumb|right|An osculating circle]]
The [[osculating circle]] and [[osculating sphere]] define [[curvature]]-equivalent radii at a particular [[point of tangency]] for [[plane figure]]s and solid figures, respectively.
